intro: Safety is the question WashU students and parents search more than any other, and most of what ranks for it is either a national crime-statistics site with zero local context or a forum thread from someone who visited once. Here is a more useful answer.

The honest truth: the neighborhoods where WashU students live are lived in by thousands of students every year, safety varies block by block more than neighborhood by neighborhood, and the most common problems students actually report are property crimes like car break-ins, not the headlines that make out-of-state parents nervous. That is not a guarantee, and this page will not pretend to offer one. What it offers is how to evaluate a specific address like someone who lives here.
directAnswer: The neighborhoods where WashU students live off campus, including University City, the Delmar Loop area, and Skinker-DeBaliviere, house thousands of students every year. Safety varies more block by block than neighborhood by neighborhood, so evaluate the specific address: visit at night, read reviews from students who lived there, and check official crime data rather than relying on reputation.

faqs.q: Is University City safe for students?
faqs.a: Large parts of University City are classic student and family neighborhoods that have housed WashU students for generations. Like any urban area it is not uniform, which is why the block matters more than the label. Visit the specific address in the evening, talk to current tenants, and read the reviews on the listing. For data, check official sources like the University City Police Department and WashU's annual campus security reports rather than commercial crime-score sites, which often lack local context.

faqs.q: What crime do students actually deal with?
faqs.a: In student discussions the recurring, realistic issues are property crimes: car break-ins, package theft, and occasional bike theft. Students who keep cars empty of visible items, use building or off-street parking where available, and get renters insurance handle most of the practical risk. Violent crime against students is rare in the areas students live, though not nonexistent anywhere in any city.

faqs.q: What safety resources does WashU provide?
faqs.a: WashU operates its own police department with patrols extending into the neighborhoods where students live, campus shuttles that run into the surrounding blocks, and a safe-ride style transportation option for getting home at night. Living near a shuttle stop is a genuine safety amenity, and every Proximity listing shows the walk time to the nearest stop.

faqs.q: How do I evaluate a specific apartment for safety?
faqs.a: Five checks: visit the block after dark, not just at noon. Ask the current tenants directly what the block is like. Read the reviews on the listing, where students mention security issues when they exist. Look at the building itself: working entry locks, lighting, and whether ground-floor windows are secured. And check where the nearest shuttle stop is if you will be walking home at night.

faqs.q: Should safety concerns keep me from living off campus?
faqs.a: For most students, no. Thousands of WashU students live off campus every year, and the practical habits above cover most of the real risk. If safety is a top concern for you or your family, prioritize buildings with controlled entry and parking, blocks close to shuttle stops, and places where reviews from previous student tenants exist so you are not guessing.

benchmarkNote: This page offers practical guidance, not guarantees or rankings. For crime data, consult official sources: the University City and St. Louis police departments and WashU's published annual security reports. Proximity does not score or rank neighborhoods by safety.
